name: Sadness
preview_text: ความรู้สึกเศร้าในร่างกายของคุณ ไม่ว่าจะเป็นหน้าอกที่แน่นจนทำให้คุณถอนหายใจ หรือความว่างเปล่าที่ว่างเปล่าที่ทำให้คุณร้องไห้และเหนื่อยล้า เป็นแผนที่ที่บอกแนวทางปฏิบัติของ TCM
categories: ["อารมณ์ ความวิตกกังวล และสุขภาพทางอารมณ์"]
synonyms: ["sSadness", "Feeling of sadness or wanting to cry", "Unexplained Sadness or Crying"]
conventional_description: In Western medicine, sadness is a normal emotional response to loss, disappointment, or stress. When it becomes persistent, pervasive, and interferes with daily life, it may be diagnosed as a depressive disorder-such as major depressive disorder, persistent depressive disorder, or adjustment disorder with depressed mood. Diagnosis relies on clinical interviews and symptom checklists, focusing on duration, severity, and impact on functioning. Sadness often brings other symptoms like fatigue, sleep changes, appetite changes, and difficulty concentrating.
conventional_treatments: First-line treatments for depression-related sadness include psychotherapy such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) or interpersonal therapy, and antidepressant medications-most commonly SSRIs (e.g., fluoxetine, sertraline) or SNRIs. For situational sadness or grief, supportive counseling or time-limited therapy may be recommended. Lifestyle measures like regular exercise, sleep hygiene, and stress reduction are also encouraged.
tcm_understanding:
TCM understands sadness primarily through the Liver and Heart organ systems. The Liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi (vital function) throughout the body, and emotional stress-especially unexpressed grief or frustration-can cause that flow to stagnate. This stagnation creates the classic tight chest, frequent sighing, and irritability that often accompany sadness. In TCM, the Liver is like the body's traffic controller; when it's stuck, everything backs up.
The Heart houses the Shen (Spirit or mind), and it needs ample Blood to anchor the Shen calmly. Prolonged sadness, overthinking, or poor nutrition can drain the Spleen's ability to produce Blood, leaving the Heart undernourished. This leads to a different kind of sadness: weepy, anxious, with palpitations and a feeling of fragility. The Spleen and Heart together govern our ability to feel grounded and nourished; when they're depleted, sadness feels like exhaustion.
Sometimes sadness brings both stagnation and deficiency at once. When Liver Qi stagnation and Heart Blood deficiency combine, you feel emotionally stuck, with chest tightness and frequent sighing, but also tearful and fragile, with palpitations. This pattern, Heart Blood Deficiency with Liver Qi Stagnation, requires addressing both the blockage and the depletion.
Other patterns can develop as sadness persists. Stagnant Liver Qi can generate Heat and turn into Fire, making the sadness more irritable and agitated, with a bitter taste and red face. Sadness can also impair the Spleen's fluid metabolism, creating Phlegm that lodges in the throat as a lump sensation (globus). Over years, sadness can consume the body's Yin (cooling, moistening essence), leading to a hollow, restless sadness with night sweats and a dry mouth. So in TCM, the quality of your sadness-tight or empty, hot or heavy-points directly to which organ systems need help.
classical_translation: "Sadness causes Qi to dissipate and become exhausted."
classical_source:
Huang Di Nei Jing, Su Wen  ,  Chapter 39, Ju Tong Lun (On Pain) 									·
More references
tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking what the sadness feels like and how it shows up in the body. Is it a dull, heavy ache in the chest that makes you sigh, or a restless, tearful emptiness? The quality of the mood and its physical companions are the first clues that steer the diagnosis toward one pattern or another.
When sadness brings sighing, chest or rib-side distension, and a mood that fluctuates with stress, the root is Liver Qi Stagnation. If that stagnation simmers into heat, the picture changes to irritability, a bitter taste, headaches, and a red tongue with a yellow coating - signs of Stagnant Liver Qi turning into Fire. The pulse shifts from wiry to wiry and rapid, confirming the heat.
A person who feels weepy, mentally restless, and emotionally “stuck” while also noticing palpitations and a pale tongue often has Heart Blood Deficiency with Liver Qi Stagnation. If instead the dominant notes are fatigue, poor appetite, loose stools, and a tendency to cry from sheer exhaustion, the pattern is Heart and Spleen Qi and Blood Deficiency. Here the pulse is weak and the tongue pale and puffy, revealing a deeper depletion.
When sadness comes with a sensation of a lump in the throat that cannot be swallowed, chest oppression, and a heavy, dulled emotional state, Qi-Phlegm is suspected. The tongue coat becomes thick and greasy, and the pulse feels slippery. In chronic cases where sadness lingers alongside palpitations, dizziness, dry mouth, night sweats, and a red tongue with little coating, the diagnosis points to Heart and Kidney Yin Deficiency, a deeper, more long-standing pattern.

patterns.symptoms: ["Frequent sighing", "Chest or rib-side tightness and distension", "Irritability alternating with low mood", "Breast tenderness or distension", "Irregular or painful menstruation"]
patterns.worse_with: Stress and frustration, Suppressing emotions or bottled-up feelings, Sedentary lifestyle, Greasy or heavy foods, Alcohol
patterns.better_with: Exercise and movement, Deep breathing or meditation, Expressing emotions openly, Aromatherapy with mint or citrus, Warmth on the rib area
patterns.why_this_happens: Sadness directly impairs the Liver's job of keeping Qi flowing freely. When that flow gets stuck, pressure builds in the chest and rib area, making you feel tight and distended. You may find yourself sighing often - it is the body's natural attempt to release the trapped Qi. The stagnation also locks up your emotions, so you swing between feeling low and irritable, without the usual smooth emotional release.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Normal or slightly dark body, red or slightly purple sides, thin white coat. Pulse: Wiry (弦 xián), taut like a guitar string, especially at the left middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Movement physically unblocks Qi, while deep breathing releases the diaphragm and helps Liver Qi rise smoothly. Expressing emotions prevents the internal pressure that causes stagnation. Stress, frustration, and emotional suppression are the direct causes of Liver Qi Stagnation, so they make it worse. A sedentary lifestyle allows Qi to pool and stagnate, while greasy foods and alcohol burden the Spleen and Liver, further clogging the flow.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Move your body every day - a brisk walk, gentle yoga, or dancing helps Qi flow. Eat light, warm meals with aromatic herbs like mint, basil, or fennel; avoid heavy, greasy foods that bog down Qi. Make time to express your feelings, whether through talking, journaling, or creative outlets, so emotions don't build up inside.

patterns.why_this_happens:
Sadness is a natural emotion, but when it lingers it can drain the Heart's blood, which houses the mind (Shen). Without enough blood to anchor it, the mind becomes restless, leading to tearfulness, palpitations, and a fragile emotional state.
At the same time, the sadness causes the Liver's Qi to become stuck, creating a sense of tightness in the chest, frequent sighing, and mood swings as the body tries to release the pressure.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin body with possible reddish sides, thin white coating. Pulse: fine (细 xì) and wiry (弦 xián), especially weak at the left cun (Heart) position and taut at the left guan (Liver) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work:
Emotional stress and bottled-up feelings directly worsen Liver Qi stagnation, which is the driving force behind the chest tightness and sighing. Overwork and lack of sleep deplete Heart Blood, leaving the mind unanchored and making tearfulness and palpitations worse.
Warm, cooked foods support the Spleen to generate Blood, which nourishes the Heart and calms the spirit. Gentle movement and deep breathing encourage the smooth flow of Liver Qi without exhausting the body, while talking or journaling releases pent-up emotions, preventing them from stagnating further.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle:
Eat warm, cooked foods that nourish Blood, such as red dates, goji berries, dark leafy greens, and small amounts of organic meat. Avoid cold, raw, and processed foods that weaken the Spleen and hinder Blood production.
Gentle daily movement like walking, tai chi, or yoga helps circulate Qi without depleting energy. Practice deep breathing or meditation to calm the mind, and consider journaling or talking with a trusted friend to express bottled-up emotions.

patterns.why_this_happens: Prolonged sadness and overthinking directly weaken the Spleen, the organ that transforms food into Qi and Blood. When Spleen Qi is depleted, the body cannot produce enough Blood to nourish the Heart. The Heart relies on abundant Blood to house the Mind (Shen); without it, the Mind becomes unsettled, leading to a persistent low mood, tearfulness, and a feeling of being emotionally fragile yet exhausted.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, with teeth marks and a thin white coating. Pulse: fine (thin) and weak, especially at the left Cun (Heart) and right Guan (Spleen) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen needs regular, warm meals to produce Qi and Blood; overthinking and worry directly weaken the Spleen and consume Heart Blood. Rest and sleep allow the body to replenish Qi and Blood, while cold foods and irregular eating habits further impair the Spleen's digestive fire, deepening the deficiency.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat regular, warm, cooked meals to support Spleen Qi-think soups, stews, and congees. Include blood-nourishing foods like red dates, goji berries, and dark leafy greens. Avoid raw, cold, or iced foods and drinks. Prioritize rest and gentle movement like walking or tai chi; avoid overthinking and mental strain, especially before bed.

patterns.pattern_name: Stagnant Liver Qi turning into Fire
patterns.symptoms: ["Irritability and angry outbursts", "Bitter taste in the mouth", "Throbbing or distending headache", "Red eyes", "Rib-side distension and pain"]

patterns.why_this_happens: Sadness initially causes Liver Qi to stagnate, like a traffic jam in the body's flow. When that stagnation persists, the pent-up energy generates Heat, which can flare upward as Fire. This internal Fire is what turns the quiet sadness into irritability, a bitter taste in the mouth, and a throbbing headache.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body (especially sides), yellow dry coating, possible prickles on sides or tip. Pulse: wiry (xian) and rapid (shu).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress and anger further stagnate Liver Qi and fan the flames of Fire, while spicy, greasy foods and alcohol add Heat to the body. Cooling foods, calming practices, and gentle movement help clear Heat and smooth the Liver's flow, directly counteracting the pattern's core mechanism.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat cooling foods like celery, cucumber, and chrysanthemum tea. Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, and cut back on alcohol and coffee. Gentle daily exercise like walking or yoga helps Qi flow, and a consistent wind-down routine before bed can prevent the Fire from disturbing sleep.

patterns.why_this_happens: When sadness lingers, the Liver's ability to keep Qi moving smoothly becomes stuck. This stagnation impairs the Spleen's job of transforming fluids, allowing dampness to accumulate and condense into Phlegm. The Phlegm then rises and lodges in the throat and chest, creating a sensation of a lump that cannot be swallowed or coughed up. This physical obstruction mirrors the emotional stuckness, deepening the feeling of heaviness and sadness.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal-coloured body, possibly slightly swollen, with a white greasy or slippery coating. Pulse: wiry (Xian) and slippery (Hua).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Brooding and stress cause Liver Qi to stagnate further, which impairs fluid metabolism and thickens Phlegm, directly worsening the throat lump and chest tightness. Damp, greasy, and cold foods burden the Spleen and create more Phlegm, adding to the obstruction. Movement and stretches help unblock Qi flow, while warm drinks and acupuncture dissolve Phlegm and soothe the Liver. Expressing emotions releases the internal pressure that feeds the cycle, preventing the physical sensation from taking hold.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked, and lightly spiced foods; avoid cold, raw, greasy, and dairy-heavy meals that create more Phlegm. Gentle daily movement like walking or qigong helps keep Qi and fluids moving. Practice expressing emotions rather than swallowing them down - journaling or talking with a friend can prevent the 'lump' from forming.

patterns.symptoms: ["Low-grade persistent sadness with mental restlessness and anxiety", "Night sweats and five-centre heat (warm palms, soles, chest)", "Palpitations and insomnia with vivid, disturbing dreams", "Low back soreness, dizziness, and tinnitus", "Dry mouth and throat, especially at night"]
patterns.worse_with: Overwork and lack of sleep, Chronic stress and worry, Spicy, fried, or heating foods, Excessive talking or mental strain
patterns.better_with: Early, consistent bedtime, Cooling foods and drinks, Gentle exercise or movement, Quiet, dark environment at night
patterns.why_this_happens: When sadness lingers for months or years, it slowly uses up the body's cooling, nourishing Yin fluids, especially those of the Heart and Kidneys. The Heart Yin anchors the mind; without it, the mind grows restless and ungrounded, producing a hollow, persistent sadness, anxiety, and sleep that never feels deep. The Kidneys supply the essence that supports the brain and ears, so as Kidney Yin dwindles, dizziness, tinnitus, and forgetfulness set in, deepening the sense of emptiness.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, especially at the tip, thin body, scanty or absent coating, dry surface, possible cracks. Pulse: thin (细 xì) and rapid (数 shuò), weak at the left Kidney position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yin is the body's cooling, restorative substance. Late nights, overwork, and stress burn through it like a candle burning at both ends, leaving the Heart and Kidneys depleted - and the sadness that comes with that emptiness deepens. Cooling, moistening foods and adequate rest replenish Yin, while calming the mind stops the cycle of restless heat that disturbs sleep and mood. Gentle movement keeps Qi flowing without draining reserves, helping the spirit feel grounded rather than hollow.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritise sleep before 11 p.m., as the hours before midnight are when Yin restores itself. Eat cooling, moistening foods like pear, black sesame, walnuts, goji berries, and millet; avoid spicy, fried, or overly heating foods, as well as coffee and alcohol. Gentle movement like tai chi or restorative yoga is ideal - avoid intense, sweat-drenching exercise that further depletes Yin. A short daily meditation or quiet breathing practice helps settle the mind and conserve Heart Yin.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help with sadness?
faqs.answer: Yes, many people find acupuncture deeply calming and effective for lifting persistent sadness. Acupuncture works by moving stuck Qi, nourishing deficient organs, and calming the Shen (spirit). Points like Shenmen (HT-7) on the wrist and Taichong (LR-3) on the foot are commonly used to settle the mind and smooth the Liver. While acupuncture alone can be helpful, it is often combined with herbal medicine for more lasting results.

faqs.question: How long will I need to take Chinese herbs?
faqs.answer: It depends on the pattern. For acute, stress-related sadness (Liver Qi stagnation), a course of herbs may only be needed for 4-8 weeks. For deeper deficiency patterns where the body's reserves have been drained over years, herbs are often taken for 3-6 months to rebuild Blood and Yin. Many patients taper down to a maintenance dose or stop once their mood is stable. Your practitioner will guide you based on your progress.

faqs.question: Can I take Chinese herbs with my antidepressant medication?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes, but it's essential that both your prescribing doctor and your TCM practitioner know exactly what you're taking. Some herbs can affect liver enzymes that metabolize medications, so full disclosure is critical. The classical formulas for sadness (like Xiao Yao San or Gui Pi Tang) are generally considered safe to combine with SSRIs when monitored. Always keep an open line of communication between your healthcare providers.

faqs.question: Will I have to make big changes to my diet?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily big, but some adjustments can make a real difference. TCM generally recommends avoiding cold, raw foods and greasy, spicy foods that can worsen Liver stagnation or weaken the Spleen. Instead, favor warm, cooked meals like soups and stews. Specific foods like longan fruit, jujube dates, and lily bulb are known to calm the Shen. Your practitioner will give you tailored advice based on your pattern.

faqs.question: What if I'm already in therapy? Can TCM still help?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. TCM complements therapy beautifully. While therapy helps you process emotions and thoughts, acupuncture and herbs work on the physical level to regulate the nervous system, improve sleep, and stabilize mood. Many patients find that TCM makes them feel more resilient and better able to engage in psychological work.

faqs.question: Is it normal to cry more at first?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, as Qi begins to move and emotions that were stuck start to release, you may feel more emotional temporarily. This is often a good sign-like a storm clearing the air. However, if the crying feels overwhelming or distressing, tell your practitioner. They can adjust your treatment to be gentler.

faqs.question: How do I know if my sadness is a TCM pattern or just normal grief?
faqs.answer: In TCM, even normal grief can create temporary patterns of Qi stagnation or deficiency, but the body usually rebalances itself over time. If sadness persists for months, feels stuck, or comes with physical symptoms like chest tightness, fatigue, or loss of appetite, it's likely a pattern that could benefit from treatment. A TCM practitioner can help you distinguish between a natural emotional process and a deeper imbalance.

research.title: Acupuncture for depression
research.description: A Cochrane systematic review of 64 trials (n=4,016) assessing acupuncture for depression. The review found moderate-quality evidence that acupuncture is more effective than no treatment or control, and that it is at least as effective as counselling. Adverse events were rare.
research.periodical: Smith CA, Armour M, Lee MS, Wang LQ, Hay PJ. Acupuncture for depression. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2018, Issue 3. Art. No.: CD004046.

research.title: Xiao Yao San for depressive disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: A meta-analysis of 27 RCTs (n=2,638) comparing Xiao Yao San to placebo or antidepressants. Xiao Yao San significantly reduced depression scores and had a lower rate of adverse events than selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. The study supports its use for mild to moderate depression.
research.periodical: Zhang Y, Han M, Liu Z, Wang J, He Q, Liu J. Xiao Yao San for depressive disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Ethnopharmacology. 2019; 237: 108-119.

research.title: Gui Pi Tang for depression and anxiety: a systematic review
research.description: A review of 12 RCTs evaluating Gui Pi Tang, alone or with antidepressants, for depression and anxiety. The formula consistently improved symptoms of sadness, insomnia, and fatigue, and was well tolerated. Limitations included small sample sizes and lack of blinding in most trials.
research.periodical: Lai J, Ma S, Wang Y, et al. Gui Pi Tang for depression and anxiety: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2017; 2017: 4020362.
